title: Floquet engineering of competing antiferromagnetism and $d$-wave superconductivity on the square lattice
abstract: We propose a driven Lieb--Hubbard quantum simulator whose prethermal dynamics realize a square-lattice spin-1/2 fermion model with independently tunable repulsive on-site and attractive bond interactions. Periodically modulating the charge-transfer offset between the site ($d$) and bond ($p$) orbitals of the Lieb lattice brings a $p$-orbital doublon energetically close to a pair in the $d$ manifold while keeping all $p$-orbital singlons off resonance, thereby creating a synthetic ``negative-$U$'' center on a Lieb-lattice bond site. Two controlled eliminations then generate a compact bond attraction in the reduced $d$-only model on the square lattice, despite the microscopic repulsion in the $p$ orbital. The resulting interaction $J$ is tunable independently of the Hubbard repulsion $U_d$ on the $d$ orbitals, while interference between photon-assisted paths provides access to an intermediate-coupling regime in which $J$ and $U_d$ are both comparable to the effective hopping. At half filling, a mean-field calculation in this regime finds adjacent antiferromagnetic and $d$-wave superconducting phases, as well as narrow coexistence regions, suggesting close competition between these orders. We discuss the branch-preparation, prethermal, and higher-band conditions required to translate the formal construction into an optical-lattice protocol. More broadly, our work identifies a structural similarity between Floquet systems and electron-phonon problems that may guide the design of novel quantum-simulation protocols.
summary: This work proposes using a periodically driven Lieb-Hubbard quantum simulator to engineer an effective model on a square lattice. By tuning the drive parameters, the authors create a controllable bond attraction that allows for the independent tuning of superconducting and repulsive interactions. This setup enables the theoretical mapping of the competition between antiferromagnetism and d-wave superconductivity, mimicking key physics in cuprate superconductors.
main_problem: The paper aims to engineer a controllable quantum simulator to study the competition between antiferromagnetism (AF) and d-wave superconductivity (dSC), a central puzzle in high-temperature superconductivity.
main_result: The derived effective model predicts a mean-field phase diagram showing adjacent regimes of sSC, dSC, and AF, suggesting a close competition between these orders.
method: The authors use Floquet engineering on a Lieb-Hubbard model, followed by successive Schrieffer-Wolff transformations to derive an effective, tunable d-only model.
model_or_system: The system is a driven Lieb-Hubbard quantum simulator realized in optical lattices. The effective model is a two-channel lattice Feshbach model describing fermions on a square lattice, with tunable bond attraction ($J$) and on-site repulsion ($U_d$).
key_observables: Phase diagram showing sSC, dSC, AF, and coexistence regions; the pairing kernel $V(k, k')$ separating into $A_{1g}$ and $B_{1g}$ channels.
important_parameters: Tunability of $J$ and $U_d$ independently; access to an intermediate-coupling regime where $J \sim U_d \sim t_{	ext{eff}}$; the ratio $J/t_{	ext{eff}}$ and $U_d/t_{	ext{eff}}$.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on second-order perturbation theory and specific energy hierarchies (e.g., $\Delta \gg \delta_R \gg t^2/\Delta$). The final phase diagram is based on mean-field calculations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the mechanism of creating a bond attraction via modulating the charge-transfer gap. Figure 3 shows the mean-field phase diagram mapping out various superconducting and magnetic orders.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the driven Lieb-Hubbard model and the mechanism for generating an effective bond attraction. It then uses perturbation theory to derive the effective d-only Hamiltonian. Finally, it analyzes the resulting model via mean-field theory to map out the competing ordered phases.
why_interesting: The use of Floquet engineering to engineer specific, tunable interactions (like negative-U centers) in a lattice system is highly relevant to AMO physics and open quantum systems, providing a clean platform to study strongly correlated phenomena.
